new_statements.quote: Bearing in mind what has been said about the vowels, the native tendency to lengthen the last vowel of a word, the native desire to give each vowel its own sound, apart from the exceptions noted above, the whole matter of accentuation resolves itself into the number of syllables in a word. Words of one syllable may be pronounced sharply, as mau, small, or as mau'u, having the same meaning. Words of two syllables take the accent on the last syllable, as do words of three syllables. Words of four syllables may take the accent on the third syllable, as enaváka, had gone, or on the last syllable, as enavaká, will go at any time, as distinguished from "I will go at the time understood."
new_statements.citation: Holmes, John H. 1913. A Preliminary Study of the Namau Language, Purari Delta, Papua. Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland 43: 124-142.
new_statements.locator: section 'Accent', pp. 127-128 (PDF pages 4-5 of the Rosetta scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19-page image-only Rosetta scan, archive.org rosettaproject_iar_morsyn-2) and re-rendered PDF pages 4-5 myself: they are the article's pp. 127-128 (running heads 'Namau Language, Purari Delta, Papua. 127' and '128 Rev. J. H. Holmes.-A Preliminary Study of the'), identical to the held renders /. The titled section 'Accent.' begins at the foot of p. 127 and the quoted passage is there word for word: 'Bearing in mind what has been said about the vowels, the native tendency to lengthen the last vowel of a word, the native desire to give each vowel its own sound, apart from the exceptions noted above, the whole matter of accentuation resolves itself into the number of syllables in a word…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the final syllable of two- and three-syllable words. In four-syllable words it falls either on the third syllable (the penult) or on the final syllable, and the choice carries a grammatical (tense/aspect) difference: enaváka 'had gone' vs enavaká 'will go at any time'. Monosyllables may be pronounced sharply or with a lengthened/duplicated final vowel. Holmes prefaces this with the admission that he cannot state concise rules and that in casual speech words are so contracted that the accent is hard to catch; final vowels are also lengthened or duplicated for emphasis.
new_statements.exceptions: Four-syllable words: accent may be on the third (penultimate) or the last syllable, with a tense/aspect contrast (enaváka vs enavaká). Holmes also notes casual-speech contraction that obscures accent, and the 'exceptions noted above' concern vowel elision (marea ai > mareai) and emphasis-lengthening of final vowels.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('the number of syllables in a word'), from a 1913 missionary description of careful/citation speech; the author explicitly says connected casual speech gives little help. Earlier scan said this article had no stress statement — that was an error.
new_statements.identity_note: Holmes 1913 describes 'Namau', the language of the whole Purari delta (Koriki, I'ai, Kaimare, Vaimuru, Maipua; also the Kaura and Muru upriver), which he says has negligible dialect variation; this is pura1257 itself (Glottolog alternative names Namau, Koriki, Iai, Maipua, Evorra), no separate dialect glottocode. 'Baimuru' in Petterson 2019 is the same language. Note the archive.org Rosetta item rosettaproject_iar_morsyn-1 is misfiled (it is Iai/Iaai of the Loyalty Islands).

sources.locator: section 'Accent', pp. 127-128 (PDF pages 4-5 of the Rosetta scan)
sources.note: Titled section 'Accent', pp. 127-128: author cannot give concise rules, but states that accent depends on syllable count — 2- and 3-syllable words accent the last syllable; 4-syllable words take accent on the third or the last syllable, the choice distinguishing tense/aspect (enaváka 'had gone' vs enavaká 'will go at any time'); monosyllables may be pronounced sharply or with lengthened final vowel (mau ~ mau'u). Also notes a native tendency to lengthen/duplicate the final vowel of a word for emphasis. Earlier world-scan note claiming 'zero hits for stress/accent' in this article is wrong.

sources.citation: Brown, Herbert A. 1973. The Eleman language family. In K. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics C-26), pp. 279-376.
sources.note: Namau (Purari)-Eleman comparison is lexical and morphological (postpositions, pronouns, tense suffixes); grep for stress/accent/tone yields nothing relevant to Purari.

Phonology tables cite Holmes 1913; 'non-tonal' line cites Petterson 2019; no stress information. Confirms dialect set (Koriki, I'ai, Maipua, Baroi/Evorra, Kaimari, Vaimuru) and that Kairi & Kolia 1977 is 'further reading'.

sources.citation: Petterson, Robert. 2019. Interesting features of Porome, an isolate language of PNG. Slides presented at the LSPNG 2019 conference (LSPNG 2019 proceedings page, langlxmelanesia.com).

sources.note: About Porome; for 'Baimuru' (= Purari) gives only an inventory count (5 vowels, 7 consonants, no /h/, has /ʔ/) and states that all neighbouring languages are tonal 'except Baimuru'. Nothing on Purari stress.

sources.citation: Franklin, Karl J. 1973. Other language groups in the Gulf District and adjacent areas. In K. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics C-26), pp. 261-278. doi 10.15144/PL-C26.261.
sources.note: Section 7.46 'Comments on phonology and grammar' covers only the Inland Gulf languages; Purari appears only in lexicostatistics and a Kibiri-Purari cognate list (7.5, 7.51). Nothing on Purari stress.

sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1907. Grammar Notes on the Namau Language spoken in the Purari Delta. In Reports of the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition to Torres Straits, vol. III (Linguistics), pp. 325-332.
sources.note: Phonology paragraph (p. 325) lists vowels and consonants and remarks only that Holmes' primer prints 'é for a strongly accented e'; no statement of where accent falls. Based entirely on Holmes' 1902 primer, not on fieldwork.
